title: The part Chinese AI could play in predicting extreme weather
source_used: Eco-Business (republishing a Dialogue Earth interview feature)
key_facts: The piece says Chinese AI weather models, including Fengwu, Pangu-Weather and Fuxi, are cheap and fast and appear to lead the field.
AI forecasting takes minutes and about a thousandth of the compute of conventional physics-based forecasts, per the article.

In July 2023 Fengwu predicted Typhoon Doksuri's path 24 hours ahead with an error of 38.7 km; the China Meteorological Administration's Mazu early-warning system, released July 2025, is used in over two dozen countries.

Models struggle with typhoon intensity, severe convective storms and extreme rainfall; in the August 2025 Yuzhong, Gansu flash flood that killed 32 people neither AI nor conventional models forecast the rainfall.
A study by Zhang Zhongwei (Karlsruhe Institute of Technology) found popular AI models systematically underestimated the frequency and intensity of record-breaking events.
Experts note data gaps in remote and Global South areas, the 'black box' nature of models and a need for verification standards.
quote_evidence: Currently, AI global weather forecasting models do particularly well on mid-range, large-scale atmospheric circulation
if it isn’t in their datasets, they can’t predict it happening
Further discussions are still needed regarding the verification procedures and standards for AI-based weather forecasting
why_it_matters_hint: Cheap AI forecasts could help poorer countries, but extreme events remain the weak spot.
notes: Explainer feature; the text says 'Dialogue Earth spoke to the experts', so the first reporter is Dialogue Earth. Mix of old and new background; no single new event.
